RCW 82.08.206; WAC 458-20-285; WORKING FAMILIES TAX CREDIT –
FEDERAL EARNED INCOME TAX CREDIT ADJUSTED GROSS INCOME
THRESHOLD - QUALIFYING CHILDREN TIEBREAKER RULES: When two
separate parents claim the same two qualifying children on their individual
Working Families Tax Credit Applications, only the parent with whom the child
lived the longest during the year is entitled to the claim the child for income
threshold purposes per the Department’s “tie-breaker” rules.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Doering, T.R.O. – An individual contests an assessment under the Department’s Working Families
Tax Credit program for the 2022 tax year, arguing the Department incorrectly removed two
qualifying children from Applicant’s application. We deny the petition.1
ISSUES
1. Under RCW 82.08.0206 and WAC 458-20-285, does an individual meet the eligibility
requirements for the Working Families Tax Credit [(WFTC)] when another party
previously claimed the same two qualifying children for the same tax year?
2. Whether an individual is entitled to a penalty waiver under RCW 82.32.105 and WAC 458-
20-228.
1 Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

FINDINGS OF FACT
. . . (Applicant) is an individual residing in Washington. On April 14, 2023, the Department
received Applicant’s WFTC application for the 2022 tax year (Tax Year). In the application,
Applicant reported earned income of $ . . . for the Tax Year and claimed two qualifying children.
On May 8, 2023, the Department’s automated system approved Applicant’s WFTC application for
the Tax Year and issued Applicant a refund of $ . . . . After Applicant received the refund, the
Department’s WFTC Division manually reviewed the application and determined that they needed
more information to confirm that Applicant was, in fact, entitled to the refund [they] already
received. On June 13, 2023, the Department sent Applicant a request for more information related
to the residency of the two qualifying children [they] claimed because another party had claimed
the same children on a separate WFTC application . . . . On June 14, 2023, the Department also
sent Applicant a request for a copy of Applicant’s 2022 federal income tax return with a copy of
the schedule EIC . . . .
On September 13, 2023, the Department sent a Notice of Balance Due in the amount of $. . . with
a due date of March 13, 2024, to Applicant after a manual review showed the qualifying children
were also claimed by the children’s other parent. . . . The Department reviewed a parenting plan
showing proof of residency and guardianship provided on the other parent’s WFTC application
and determined that the other parent was the custodial parent for the purposes of the [Earned
Income Tax Credit] (EITC) and removed them from Applicant’s account. Based on that
documentation, the Department determined that Applicant and the children’s other parent ceased
to live in the same place on December 1, 2022, and on December 2, 2022, the children resided
with the children’s other parent the remaining days of the Tax Year. The Department then reduced
Applicant’s WFTC from $ . . . to $ . . . due to the removal of the qualifying children.
On October 27, 2023, a second Notice of Balance due was issued showing a balance due of $ . . .
and a due date of March 13, 2024, . . . . On December 1, 2023, the Department sent Applicant a
notice stating their application had been denied due to a failure to provide the additional
information requested . . . .
On March 1, 2024, Applicant provided a copy of their 2022 tax transcript. On March 15, 2024, the
Department issued a third Notice of Balance Due in the amount of $. . . showing an increased
WFTC overpayment of $. . . , an assessment penalty in the amount of $. . . , and interest in the
amount of $. . . due to the rejection of Applicant’s application on December 1, 2024, and
Applicant’s failure to pay the assessment before the due date. . . . . On March 27, 2024, the
Department determined that Applicant had excluded their self-employment income from their
WFTC application and added $. . . of self-employment income with a $. . . tax deduction, bringing
their total income for the Tax Year to $ . . . .
On May 22, 2024, Applicant submitted a Petition for Review. Applicant argues in their petition,
“both Mom & Dad claimed kids, when children lived with both Mom & Dad[.] Dad paid all
medical, childcare, and name was on home lease. Copies of proof turned in already.” Taxpayer’s
Petition, pg. 3. Applicant did not request a hearing on their petition.

On June 14, 2024, the Department sent a request for additional information as Applicant’s Petition
for Review did not include any additional documentation to support Taxpayer’s arguments. . . .
The Department stated in the request, “to preserve our jurisdiction over your petition for review
we will accept the document dated May 21, 2024, as timely filed. However, a petition for review
must comply with WAC 458-20-100, which requires an adequate statement of facts and reasons
for the review and documents supporting the [applicant’s] position. Such information is necessary
in order for us to better evaluate your case.” Id. Applicant did not respond to this request for more
information and the Department was unable to make contact [with] Applicant.
ANALYSIS
1. Eligibility for Working Families Tax Credit
The WFTC is a tax credit provided to eligible low-income persons in the form of a refund of retail
sales and use taxes paid after January 1, 2022. RCW 82.08.0206(1). The Department calculates an
applicant’s WFTC refund amount based on the applicant’s “properly filed federal income tax
return for the period for which [the applicant is] claiming the refund.” WAC 458-20-285 (“Rule
285”), Answer 10C.
The definition of an “eligible low-income person” is composed of five elements. See generally
RCW 82.08.0206; Rule 285, Part 1.
1. The individual must have a valid Social Security number (“SSN”) or Individual Taxpayer
Identification number (“ITIN”). Rule 285(1)(a).
2. The individual must have properly filed a federal income tax return for the prior federal tax
year. RCW 82.08.0206(2)(a)(i)(B); Rule 285(1)(b).
3. The individual generally must be eligible for the federal EITC provided in Title 26 U.S.C.
Sec. 32 of the Internal Revenue Code, “including meeting the federal income thresholds,”
regardless of whether the individual actually claimed or received the EITC.2 RCW
82.08.0206(2)(a)(1)(A); Rule 285(1)(c).
4. The individual must have been a Washington resident during the year for which the
individual claims the WFTC. Rule 285(1)(d).
5. The individual must have paid Washington sales or use tax on taxable purchases made
during the tax year for which the individual claims the refund. Rule 285(1)(e).
Here, the primary element of this dispute is whether Applicant meets the federal income thresholds
to be eligible for the EITC. Specifically, the issue before us is whether Applicant’s two children
are “qualifying children” under the rules of the EITC. As such, this analysis will primarily address
that element.
To qualify for the EITC, an applicant’s income “must be below the federal adjusted gross income
(AGI) threshold . . . .” Rule 285(4). If the applicant’s AGI is “at or above the federal income
threshold, [the applicant is] not eligible for the EITC” and, therefore, ineligible for the WFTC.
2 An individual will meet this element if the individual or the individual’s spouse or qualifying children “have a valid ITIN instead
of a SSN, which is not permitted under federal EITC eligibility requirements.” Rule 285(1)(c).

Det. No. 24-0266, 45 WTD 118 (June 9, 2026) 121
Rule 285(4). The AGI threshold for a single person with no qualifying children for the Tax Year
is $16,480 while the AGI threshold for a single person with two qualifying children is $49,399. ..
Rule 285, Answer 10(E).
Here, Applicant’s earned income as initially reported on their WFTC application was $. . . , which
was below both limits. However, the Department later determined that Applicant’s income was,
in fact, $. . . after analyzing Applicant’s federal tax transcript for the Tax Year. This increase puts
Applicant’s income over the threshold for a single person with no qualifying children. Applicant
has made no argument that the Department incorrectly increased Applicant’s income for the Tax
Year. Thus, Applicant will only qualify for the EITC, and consequently, the WFTC, if they are
able to claim their children as qualifying children. As such, our analysis now turns to whether
Applicant may claim these two children as qualifying children for the purposes of the EITC and
WFTC.
In situations where several people could potentially claim the same qualifying child, the
Department must use the following hierarchy of “tie breaker” rules set forth in Rule 285 to
determine who can claim the child:
(a) If only one person is the child’s legal parent (“parent”): The parent may claim
the child;
(b) If both parents file a joint tax return with each other: They may claim the child;
(c) If both parents claim the child on separate tax returns: The parent with whom
the child lived with the longest during the year may claim the child;
(d) If the child lived with each parent for the same amount of time: The parent with
the higher AGI for the year may claim the child;
(e) If neither parent can claim the child: The person who had the highest AGI for
the year may claim the child; and
(f) If a parent can claim the child but does not: The person who had the highest AGI
for the year may claim the child, but only if that person’s AGI is greater than the
AGI of any of the child’s parents who can claim the child.
Rule 285, Answer 10H (emphasis added). See also IRS Publication 596, Rule 9.
Here, Rule 285, Answer 10(H)(a) and (b) do not apply to the Applicant’s situation. Applicant
argues that the two children lived with both parents during the tax year and that Applicant paid for
all medical care, childcare, and was the name on the lease where the children lived. However, the
Rule 285 tiebreaker rules must be strictly applied, and the analysis must only focus on who the
children lived with the most days during the Tax Year.

The other parent provided documentation with their own WFTC application that showed that the
two parents lived together from January 1, 2022, until December 1, 2022. The other parent then
had primary custody of the two children from December 2, 2022, to December 31, 2022. Applicant
has provided no documentation to refute the documentation provided by the other parent. Thus,
the two children lived with the other parent longer during the Tax Year and the Department
correctly determined the other parent was the custodial parent for purposes of the EITC and WFTC.
Therefore, Applicant was unable to claim the two children as qualifying children, Applicant did
not meet the federal income threshold to be eligible for the EITC to qualify for the WFTC, and the
Department properly issued an assessment for the full refunded amount.
2. Penalty Waiver
Taxpayers have certain rights and responsibilities under Washington law, including the
responsibility to file accurate returns and pay their taxes in a timely manner. Ch. 82.32A RCW. In
the event the Department determines that a taxpayer has paid less tax than was properly due, the
Department “shall assess against the taxpayer such additional amount found to be due.” RCW
82.32.050(1).
Whenever the Department issues an assessment for unpaid taxes, it must also include interest. Id.
Interest is calculated from the last day of the month following the final period assessed. WAC 458-
20-228(7). Upon receiving payment from a taxpayer, the Department must apply the payment to
interest and penalties first, then to tax, without regard to any direction from the taxpayer. RCW
82.32.080(5)(a).
If a taxpayer fails to pay an assessment by the due date, the Department must assess an assessment
penalty of 15 percent of the taxes due. RCW 82.32.090(2). The assessment penalty will increase
to a total of 25 percent of the taxes due if the taxpayer does not submit payment to the Department
by the 30th day following the assessment’s due date. Id.
The Department must impose interest and penalties when the conditions for imposing them are
met. RCW 82.32.090(1); Det. No. 01-193, 21 WTD 264 (2002); Det. No. 99-279, 20 WTD 149
(2001).
Here, Applicant does not argue that the penalties or interest were improperly assessed by the
Department, only that they were entitled to the WFTC. As previously determined, Applicant was
not eligible for the WFTC. Thus, the Department properly issued the assessment against Applicant
and Applicant failed to pay the assessment or request a Petition for Review before the due date of
the assessment. Therefore, the Department properly imposed the penalties and interest[] on the
assessment.
In closing, if Applicant made a mistake on their WFTC application, they could file an amended
application. Applicant can visit our website for more information at workingfamiliescredit.wa.gov,
or contact our call center during business hours at 360-763-7300.

DECISION AND DISPOSITION
We deny the petition.
